section_summary: This section begins with the continuation of Thomas C. Farnsworth’s strongly anti-Japanese letter about Hawaii, accompanied by newspaper clippings on Japanese military, political, and commercial expansion in China. It then documents official correspondence concerning Japanese-American political influence in Hawaii and Kilsoo K. Haan’s campaign for Korean and Chinese resistance to Japan. Haan urges moral and economic pressure against Japan, relief and intelligence work for Korean students, fortification of Guam, and revision of American neutrality policy; State Department officials acknowledge him but avoid commitments beyond established policy.

subfiles.title: Continuation of letter warning of Japanese influence in Hawaii, with newspaper enclosures
subfiles.about: Farnsworth alleges that Japanese residents and institutions threaten American political, economic, and military control of Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: The continuation attacks Japanese-language schools, religious institutions, family practices, commercial activity, landholding, fishing, remittances, and dual citizenship in Hawaii. Enclosed newspaper material reports the expatriation of University of Hawaii ROTC students and Japanese military, political, and economic expansion in China. Farnsworth concludes by opposing Hawaiian statehood, advocating commission or military government, and requesting an investigation of the Japanese population and economy.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of “Japanese Threaten to Dominate Hawaii”
subfiles.from: James K. Fisk, California Joint Immigration Committee
subfiles.about: Fisk forwards a committee release alleging a Japanese political threat in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Fisk calls the release's conditions disturbing, saying its dual-citizenship figures came from Governor Poindexter in 1936 and later figures were unavailable.

subfiles.title: Japanese Threaten to Dominate Hawaii
subfiles.about: The release uses Japanese-American population and citizenship figures to oppose Hawaiian statehood.
subfiles.summary: Committee release: a Hawaii Hochi estimate that Japanese are over a third of Hawaii's population presented as an electoral and dual-nationality threat, warning statehood could permit Japanese domination.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Fisk’s committee release
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges receipt and consideration of the release on Japanese influence in Hawaii.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton acknowledges Fisk's December 17 letter and enclosure, which received careful consideration.

subfiles.title: Introduction of Kilsoo Haan to the secretary of state
subfiles.about: Gillette introduces Kilsoo Haan as a knowledgeable source on Hawaiian and Japanese affairs.
subfiles.summary: Gillette introduces Kilsoo Haan, a valuable witness before the Hawaiian Territory Commission, as having information of possible interest to State and asks Hull for courtesy.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning a possible meeting with Kilsoo Haan
subfiles.about: Hull thanks Gillette for introducing Haan and says either he or an associate will try to receive him.
subfiles.summary: Hull notes Gillette’s statement that Haan may possess information of interest to the Department. He warns that emergency matters and exceptionally long working hours may prevent a personal meeting, but promises that an associate can meet Haan if Hull is unavailable.

subfiles.title: Washington branch organized by Kilsoo K. Haan
subfiles.about: The clipping reports the establishment of a Washington branch of the Sino-Korean Peoples League.
subfiles.summary: Clipping: Haan organized a Washington branch to oppose Japanese fascism, restrict war-material sales to Japan, and support Sino-Korean groups, while consulting departments on secret Japanese organizations.

subfiles.title: Request for an audience with Cordell Hull
subfiles.about: Haan requests a late-April audience to present a memorandum and plea.
subfiles.summary: Haan seeks an audience with Hull, preparing a memorandum, with letters of introduction from Senator Gillette and Delegate King.

subfiles.title: Response to Haan’s appointment request
subfiles.from: C. W. Gray, assistant to the secretary of state
subfiles.about: Gray advises Haan to telephone upon returning to Washington so that an appointment can be arranged.
subfiles.summary: Gray explains emergencies limit Hull's appointments, suggests Haan phone in the last week of April, and offers an appointment with an associate.

subfiles.title: Departmental abstract of Haan’s April 12 memorandum
subfiles.about: The memorandum summarizes Haan’s proposals and judges that he offers no important new information.
subfiles.summary: Abstract of Haan's April 12 memorandum: no new intelligence; he asks moral support for Chinese, Koreans and liberal Japanese, a two-year halt to war-material sales, and jobs for 250-300 Korean students in intelligence.

subfiles.title: Transmittal of Haan’s memorandum
subfiles.about: Haan encloses his memorandum of requests and renews his request for an audience.
subfiles.summary: Haan asks Hull to read the enclosed Sino-Korean Peoples League memorandum and renews his appointment request.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on American policy toward Japan, Korea, and China
subfiles.about: Haan argues for moral and economic resistance to Japanese expansion and assistance for Korean students in the United States.
subfiles.summary: Haan portrays Japanese expansion in Korea and China as an eventual threat to Hawaii, Guam, Alaska, the Philippines, and the United States, supporting his argument with historical diplomatic quotations, trade figures, press reports, and statements attributed to Japanese officials. He proposes public expressions of sympathy, a two-year prohibition on war-material exports to Japan accompanied by federal purchases for American defense, and cooperation between Sino-Korean organizations and American intelligence agencies. He also asks that roughly 300 Korean students be allowed to remain as political refugees and be considered for intelligence work. The memorandum concludes that resistance by Koreans, Chinese, liberal Japanese, and the United States could prevent a broader racial and military conflict in the Pacific.

subfiles.title: Follow-up request to schedule an appointment
subfiles.about: Haan asks Gray to choose a date and time for the proposed State Department appointment.
subfiles.summary: Haan apologizes for his delayed reply to Gray's April 14 letter and asks Gray to set an appointment by letter instead of telephone.

subfiles.title: Letter enclosing testimony before the House Committee on Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Haan forwards his congressional testimony and renews his requests for State Department assistance.
subfiles.summary: Haan urges Hamilton to review his House Foreign Affairs testimony and requests, arguing Koreans in Hawaii and on the Pacific Coast could aid security and that fewer than 300 Korean students suit intelligence work.

subfiles.title: Testimony before the House Committee on Foreign Affairs
subfiles.about: Haan supports selective neutrality sanctions against aggressors and the fortification of Guam as measures to deter Japan.
subfiles.summary: Haan describes the Sino-Japanese conflict as a struggle between democracy and “Japanized Fascism” and argues that American neutrality policy materially aids Japanese expansion. Drawing parallels between Japan’s annexation of Korea and the strategic vulnerability of Guam, he endorses Senator Elbert D. Thomas’s proposal allowing the president to embargo aggressor states while permitting sales to their victims. He contends that sanctions, fortification of Guam, and a moral and economic “backfire” would strengthen Chinese, Korean, and Japanese liberal morale while protecting American Pacific possessions and future commerce.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Kilsoo K. Haan
subfiles.about: Hamilton records his meeting with Haan about Korea, economic pressure on Japan, and the status of Korean students.
subfiles.summary: Haan asked for more State interest in Koreans, economic pressure on Japan, and permission for about 300 Korean students to stay; Hamilton declined to go beyond public policy and referred him to the Visa Division.
